t: How To Handle Students Who Question Your Classroom Management nagement/
q: So when a student questions the way you manage your classroom—most often in front of the class—it can be hard not to take it personally. It can be hard not to bristle and become defensive.
Because showing frustration puts you at odds with not only the student who asked the question but with your entire class.
You calmly, even cheerfully, say your line and then move on. There is no reason to wait for a response or gird yourself for an argument.
If you can’t point to a logical reason why you have certain rules, procedures, routines, etc., then you’re asking for trouble. Because arbitrary or unexplained regulation causes resentment.
In my role coaching teachers , I find myself asking frequently “Why are you doing that? What’s the purpose?” And often they can’t tell me, which means their students don’t know either.
They don’t necessarily even have to agree. They just need to know why .
x: Linsin advises teachers on responding when a student challenges a classroom rule or procedure, often in front of the whole class.
When students question a classroom rule, reacting with frustration or defensiveness creates a 'you-against-them' dynamic with the whole class.
The recommended response is to answer calmly and cheerfully with a brief, prepared explanation and then move on without waiting for a rebuttal.
He stresses that every rule, procedure, and routine needs a clear, logical purpose that a teacher can articulate in a sentence or two; unexplained or arbitrary expectations breed resentment.
In coaching sessions, Linsin often finds teachers cannot explain the purpose behind their own practices, meaning their students don't know it either.

q: There are teachers who seem blessed with natural charisma. The lucky ones.
Whatever the reason, they become almost entirely stripped of their true personality.
This is a big problem. Because when you inhabit a teaching persona that is different from your natural self, you become uninteresting and hard for students to pay attention to.

The truth is, you are charismatic. Just as you are . In fact, it’s your uniqueness, your quirks and idiosyncrasies, your vulnerability and eccentricity, even your perceived weaknesses that are your greatest strengths.
I’m nothing special. I’m introverted by nature. I’m not a smooth talker. I’m frequently awkward. Again, doesn’t matter. In fact, these very things help endear me to my students.
Charisma is nothing more than the inward acceptance and outward expression of the best of who you really are.
x: Linsin explores why some teachers seem naturally charismatic and argues the difference is not innate talent but a single behavior: embracing one's authentic self in the classroom.

t: A Little-Known Secret To Effective Teaching
q: The split second you recognize your students doing what you want or asked of them, you clam up and allow them to experience success all on their own.

Using no sudden movements, slowly ease back and away from your class. Once you reach a distance from which you can observe every student, stay silent and in one place until the task is either finished or no longer successful.
You must never send your students off on their own unless they’ve proven to you that they know what is expected.
The reason the strategy is so effective is that whenever students experience success without interference, they gain deep confidence in themselves and their own abilities.
We’ve become conditioned to always be “teaching.” We’ve been brainwashed by the powers that be into believing that good teaching looks busy.
But to make this potentially game-changing strategy work, you must purge yourself from this falsehood.
x: Linsin describes a rarely discussed strategy: the instant a teacher notices students doing exactly what was asked, the teacher should go silent and physically withdraw, allowing students to experience success entirely…

He explains the technique step by step—easing back without sudden movement, observing from a distance, and staying silent until the task concludes—while cautioning that it only works if the teacher has already taught…
